notes.definition: When certain insulating materials are rubbed against each other, electrons are transferred from one to the other, so both become electrically charged. The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged; the material that loses electrons becomes equally positively charged. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
explanation: Atoms contain positively charged protons in the nucleus and negatively charged electrons outside it. Normally an object has equal numbers of each, so it is uncharged. When two insulating materials, such as a polythene rod and a woollen cloth, are rubbed together, friction moves electrons from one surface to the other. Only electrons move: the positive charges are protons, locked in the nuclei, and cannot be rubbed off.

The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged. The material that loses electrons is left with more protons than electrons, so it becomes positively charged. The two charges are equal in size and opposite in sign, because every electron lost by one material is gained by the other. For example, a polythene rod rubbed with a cloth gains electrons and becomes negative; an acetate (perspex) rod rubbed with a cloth loses electrons and becomes positive.

Insulators keep the charge where it was produced because electrons cannot move through them. A metal rod held in your hand would not stay charged, because electrons would flow through the metal and your body to or from the earth. This build-up of charge that stays in place on an insulator is called static electricity.

When two charged objects are brought close together, they exert a force on each other: like charges (two negatives or two positives) repel, and unlike charges (one positive, one negative) attract. These are non-contact forces, because the objects do not need to touch. Evidence comes from hanging a charged rod from a thread and bringing a second charged rod close: the hanging rod turns away from a rod with the same charge and towards a rod with the opposite charge. A rubbed balloon sticking to a wall and hair standing up after brushing are everyday examples.

If enough charge builds up on an object, the potential difference between the object and the earth (or a nearby earthed conductor, such as a metal tap or door handle) becomes very high. Electrons can then jump across the air gap, producing a spark. This is why you sometimes get a small shock when touching a car door after sliding across the seat, or a door handle after walking on a nylon carpet. Lightning is a huge spark between a charged cloud and the ground.
keyFacts: Rubbing certain insulating materials together makes them electrically charged.
Negatively charged electrons are rubbed off one material onto the other.
The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged.
The material that loses electrons becomes equally positively charged.
Only electrons move; positive charges (protons) stay in the nuclei.
Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.
The forces between charged objects are non-contact forces.
If the potential difference between a charged object and earth becomes high enough, a spark can jump across the gap.
Insulators hold static charge because electrons cannot flow through them.

keyTerms.definition: Electric charge that builds up and stays in one place on an insulator.
A negatively charged particle outside the nucleus; the only charged particle transferred by rubbing.
A material that does not allow charge to flow through it easily, so it can hold static charge.
Push apart; objects with like charges repel each other.
Pull together; objects with unlike charges attract each other.
A force between objects that are not touching, such as the electrostatic force between charged objects.
A flow of charge (electrons) across an air gap when the potential difference becomes high enough.

workedExamples.title: Charging a rod by rubbing
workedExamples.question: A polythene rod is rubbed with a woollen cloth and becomes negatively charged. Explain how the rod and the cloth become charged.
steps: Friction between the surfaces transfers electrons.
Electrons move from the cloth onto the rod.
The rod has gained electrons, so it has more electrons than protons: it is negatively charged.
The cloth has lost the same number of electrons, so it has an equal positive charge.
workedExamples.answer: Electrons move from the cloth to the rod: rod negative, cloth equally positive.

workedExamples.title: Predicting forces
workedExamples.question: A charged polythene rod (negative) hangs from a thread. A rubbed acetate rod (positive) is brought near it, then a second rubbed polythene rod is brought near. Describe what happens each time.
steps: Acetate is positive and polythene is negative: unlike charges.
Unlike charges attract, so the hanging rod turns towards the acetate rod.
The second polythene rod is negative, the same as the hanging rod: like charges.
Like charges repel, so the hanging rod turns away.
workedExamples.answer: Attracted by the acetate rod; repelled by the polythene rod.

workedExamples.title: A shock from a car door
workedExamples.question: A passenger slides across a car seat, gets out and feels a small shock when touching the metal door. Explain why.
steps: Sliding across the seat rubs the clothing and seat together.
Electrons are transferred, so the passenger becomes charged.
There is a large potential difference between the charged passenger and the earthed car.
When the hand gets close, electrons jump across the small gap: a spark, felt as a shock.
workedExamples.answer: Rubbing charges the passenger; the high pd causes a spark to the door.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think positive charges (protons) are rubbed onto the positively charged object.
misconceptions.right: In fact only electrons move. A positive object has lost electrons; it has not gained protons.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think rubbing creates charge.
misconceptions.right: In fact charge is only transferred: the electrons gained by one object equal those lost by the other, so the charges are equal and opposite.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think charged objects have to touch to exert a force.
misconceptions.right: In fact electrostatic forces are non-contact forces that act across a gap.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think metals can be charged by rubbing while held in the hand, just like insulators.
misconceptions.right: In fact charge flows away through a metal and your body to earth, so static charge builds up on insulators.

realWorld: Hair standing up after brushing, or a balloon sticking to a wall after being rubbed on a jumper.
Small shocks from car doors, trolleys and door handles after walking on nylon carpet.
Lightning is a giant spark caused by a build-up of static charge in clouds.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Physics (8463) only, not Combined Science.
Producing static electricity by rubbing insulating materials, and sparking.
Explaining static electricity in terms of the transfer of electrons.
Forces of attraction and repulsion between charged objects as non-contact forces.
examTips: Always say electrons are transferred. Never say positive charge or protons move.
State both outcomes: the object that gains electrons becomes negative; the one that loses electrons becomes positive.
For force questions, state the rule (like repel, unlike attract) and identify the charges first.
For sparking, link a build-up of charge to a large potential difference between the object and earth, then electrons jumping across the gap.
summary: Rubbing insulators transfers electrons from one to the other.
Gaining electrons makes an object negative; losing electrons makes it positive.
The charges produced are equal and opposite.
Like charges repel; unlike charges attract; these are non-contact forces.
A large build-up of charge can cause a spark to earth.

questions.question: What particles are transferred when a polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth?
markScheme: 1 mark: Electrons
questions.explanation: Only electrons are transferred. Protons and neutrons are held in the nucleus.

questions.question: An object becomes negatively charged after being rubbed. What has happened to it?
markScheme: 1 mark: It has gained electrons.
questions.explanation: A negative charge means more electrons than protons, so the object has gained electrons.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows two negatively charged balloons hanging next to each other.
What happens to the balloons?
markScheme: 1 mark: They repel.
questions.explanation: Like charges repel, so the balloons push apart.

questions.question: A positively charged rod is brought close to a negatively charged rod. What happens?
markScheme: 1 mark: They attract.
questions.explanation: Unlike charges attract.

questions.question: Which type of material can be charged by rubbing and hold its charge?
markScheme: 1 mark: An insulator
questions.explanation: Insulators keep charge in place because electrons cannot move through them.
options: A metal held in the hand

questions.question:
A rod is rubbed with a cloth. The rod becomes positively charged.
Which statement about the cloth is correct?
markScheme: 1 mark: It becomes negative with an equal charge.
questions.explanation: Electrons moved from the rod onto the cloth, so the cloth gains exactly the electrons the rod lost: an equal negative charge.
options: It becomes negative with an equal charge.
It becomes negative with a larger charge.

questions.question: Why is the force between two charged objects called a non-contact force?
markScheme: 1 mark: It acts without the objects touching.
questions.explanation: Electrostatic forces act across a gap, so the objects need not touch.
options: It only acts when they touch.
It acts only in a vacuum.
It acts without the objects touching.

questions.question: A student says 'the rod became positive because protons were rubbed onto it.' What is the correct explanation?
markScheme: 1 mark: Electrons were rubbed off it.
questions.explanation: Protons cannot move; the rod lost electrons, leaving more protons than electrons.

questions.question: Why might a person feel a shock when touching a metal door handle after walking on a nylon carpet?
markScheme: 1 mark: Charge has built up on the person, and electrons jump across the gap to the earthed handle.
questions.explanation: Walking rubs shoes on the carpet, charging the person. The pd between person and earthed handle causes a spark.
options: The handle is connected to the mains.
The carpet stores electricity like a battery.
Charge has built up on the person, and electrons jump across the gap to the earthed handle.
Protons flow from the handle to the person.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a negatively charged rod hanging from a thread.
Rod X is brought near one end of the suspended rod, and the suspended rod is repelled.
Rod Y is brought near the other end, and the suspended rod is attracted.
What are the charges on rod X and rod Y?
markScheme: 1 mark: X negative, Y positive
questions.explanation: Repulsion means like charges, so X is negative. Attraction means unlike charges, so Y is positive.

Figure 1 shows a polythene rod being rubbed with a cloth. The rod becomes negatively charged.
Explain how the polythene rod becomes negatively charged.
markScheme: 1 mark: electrons are transferred (by friction)
1 mark: from the cloth to the rod
1 mark: so the rod has more electrons than protons / gains electrons

questions.question: Give the rules for the forces between charged objects.
markScheme: 1 mark: like charges repel
1 mark: unlike (opposite) charges attract
questions.explanation: Two simple rules, both needed for full marks.

questions.question: Explain why the charges on a rubbed rod and the cloth are equal in size.
markScheme: 1 mark: the number of electrons lost by one equals the number gained by the other / charge is transferred, not created
questions.explanation: Charge is conserved, so the two objects end up with equal and opposite charges.

questions.question: Describe an experiment that shows charged objects exert forces on each other without touching.
markScheme: 1 mark: hang a charged rod from a thread (so it can turn freely)
1 mark: bring a second charged rod near without touching
1 mark: the hanging rod moves away (like charges) or towards (unlike charges)
questions.explanation: The hanging rod turns even though nothing touches it, showing a non-contact force.

questions.question: Explain why a metal rod held in the hand cannot be charged by rubbing.
markScheme: 1 mark: metal is a conductor
1 mark: electrons flow through it and the person to/from earth, so no charge builds up
questions.explanation: Charge only stays put on insulators.
acceptedAnswers: electrons flow through hand to earth

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a charged metal dome near an earthed metal sphere.
Explain how a spark is produced across the air gap.
markScheme: 1 mark: charge builds up so the potential difference between the object and earth becomes large
1 mark: electrons jump across the air gap (to earth), producing a spark
questions.explanation: When the pd is high enough, charge flows through the air as a spark.

questions.question:
An acetate rod is rubbed with a cloth. The rod becomes positively charged.
Give the charge on the cloth and explain why it has this charge.
markScheme: 1 mark: negative
1 mark: electrons moved from the rod to the cloth, so the cloth gained electrons
questions.explanation: The rod is positive because it lost electrons; they went to the cloth.

questions.question: A student rubs a balloon on her hair. Afterwards, her hair strands stand up and spread apart. Use ideas about charge to explain this.
markScheme: 1 mark: electrons are transferred between the hair and the balloon
1 mark: each strand of hair gets the same type of charge
1 mark: like charges repel, so the strands push apart
questions.explanation: All the strands lose electrons (become positive), so they repel each other and stand apart.

questions.question: Explain how rubbing two insulating materials together can produce static electricity, and describe the forces between charged objects. Use ideas about electrons in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: atoms contain protons (positive, in nucleus) and electrons (negative); uncharged objects have equal numbers; rubbing (friction) transfers electrons from one material to the other; only electrons move, protons stay in nuclei; the material gaining electrons becomes negative; the material losing electrons becomes positive; the charges are equal and opposite; insulators hold the charge because electrons cannot flow; e.g. polythene becomes negative, acetate becomes positive; like charges repel, unlike charges attract; forces are non-contact; evidence: suspended charged rod turns away/towards another charged rod; build-up of charge can lead to sparking.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed explanation of electron transfer giving both charges, why insulators hold charge, and correct description of attraction and repulsion as non-contact forces.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct idea of electron transfer and at least one correct force rule.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as 'rubbing makes things charged' or 'opposites attract'.
questions.explanation: Top answers stay precise: electrons move, the gainer is negative, the loser is equally positive, and like repel while unlike attract without contact.

questions.question: A car is refuelled at a petrol station. As fuel flows through the plastic pipe, static charge can build up. Explain why this could be dangerous and suggest how the danger can be reduced.
markScheme: Indicative content: friction between fuel and pipe transfers electrons; charge builds up on the pipe/nozzle/car; potential difference between charged object and earth increases; if large enough, a spark can jump across the gap; petrol vapour is flammable, so a spark could cause a fire or explosion; reduce danger by connecting (earthing) the nozzle/tanker with a conducting wire to earth so electrons flow away safely before charge builds up; using conducting (metal) nozzles connected to earth.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains charge build-up by friction, the spark risk with flammable vapour, and a sensible earthing method.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): identifies a spark or fire risk, or earthing, with little explanation.
questions.explanation: The danger is sparking near flammable vapour. Earthing lets charge flow away steadily so the pd never gets large enough for a spark.

questions.question: Which pair of objects would repel each other?
markScheme: 1 mark: Two positive rods
questions.explanation: Like charges repel. Two positive rods have the same type of charge.
options: A positive rod and a negative rod
A positive cloth and a negative rod
A negative balloon and a positive wall

questions.question:
Rod A and rod B are each rubbed with a separate cloth.
Table 1 shows the charge on each rod after rubbing.
The cloth used to rub rod A is then brought near rod B.
What happens?
markScheme: 1 mark: They repel, because the cloth is positive and rod B is positive.
questions.explanation: Rod A gained electrons from its cloth, so that cloth is positive. Rod B is also positive. Like charges repel.
options: They attract, because the cloth is negative.
They repel, because the cloth is positive and rod B is positive.
Nothing, because the cloth is uncharged.
They attract, because the cloth is positive and rod B is negative.

questions.question: Why does an uncharged object have no overall charge?
markScheme: 1 mark: It has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
questions.explanation: Each proton's positive charge is balanced by an electron's negative charge.
options: It has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
Its electrons are all in the nucleus.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a polythene rod being rubbed with a woollen cloth. The rod becomes negatively charged.
In which direction do electrons move?
markScheme: 1 mark: From the cloth to the rod
questions.explanation: The polythene rod becomes negative, so it must have gained electrons from the cloth.
options: From the cloth to the rod
From the rod to the cloth
Electrons do not move; protons do

questions.question: Give the type of charge carried by an electron.
markScheme: 1 mark: negative
questions.explanation: Electrons are negatively charged; protons are positively charged.

questions.question:
A rubbed rod is attracted to a negatively charged rod.
Give the charge on the rubbed rod and explain what happened to its electrons during rubbing.
markScheme: 1 mark: positive (unlike charges attract)
1 mark: it lost electrons (to the cloth) during rubbing
questions.explanation: Attraction to a negative rod shows it is positive, which means electrons were removed from it.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a thundercloud above the ground.
Use ideas about static charge to explain how lightning occurs.
markScheme: 1 mark: charge builds up in the cloud (e.g. by friction between particles)
1 mark: the potential difference between the cloud and the ground becomes very large
1 mark: charge (electrons) flows through the air as a giant spark
questions.explanation: Lightning is sparking on a huge scale: a big build-up of charge, a big pd, and a discharge through the air.
